claim: Tunneling nanotubes (TNTs) are open actin- and membrane-based channels connecting remote cells.
source: Tunneling nanotubes (TNTs) are open actin- and membrane-based channels, connecting remote cells and allowing direct transfer of cellular material (e.g. vesicles, mRNAs, protein aggregates) from the cytoplasm to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a defining characteristic of TNTs.

claim: TNTs allow direct transfer of cellular material including vesicles, mRNAs, and protein aggregates from cytoplasm to cytoplasm.
source: Tunneling nanotubes (TNTs) are open actin- and membrane-based channels, connecting remote cells and allowing direct transfer of cellular material (e.g. vesicles, mRNAs, protein aggregates) from the cytoplasm to the cytoplasm.
evidence: The abstract explicitly lists the types of cellular material transferred through TNTs.

claim: TNTs are important in pathological conditions including cancers and neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Although they are important especially, in pathological conditions (e.g. cancers, neurodegenerative diseases), their precise composition and their regulation were still poorly described.
evidence: The abstract states the importance of TNTs in pathological conditions.

claim: The precise composition and regulation of TNTs were poorly described prior to this study.
source: Although they are important especially, in pathological conditions (e.g. cancers, neurodegenerative diseases), their precise composition and their regulation were still poorly described.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this as a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: A biochemical approach was used to separate TNTs from cell bodies and from extracellular vesicles and particles (EVPs).
source: Here, using a biochemical approach allowing to separate TNTs from cell bodies and from extracellular vesicles and particles (EVPs), we obtained the full composition of TNTs compared to EVPs.
evidence: The abstract describes the methodological approach used in the study.

claim: The full protein composition of TNTs compared to EVPs was obtained.
source: Here, using a biochemical approach allowing to separate TNTs from cell bodies and from extracellular vesicles and particles (EVPs), we obtained the full composition of TNTs compared to EVPs.
evidence: The abstract states this as a key finding of the study.

claim: CD9 and CD81 tetraspanins are major components of TNTs.
source: We then focused on two major components of our proteomic data, the CD9 and CD81 tetraspanins, and further investigated their specific roles in TNT formation and function.
evidence: The abstract identifies CD9 and CD81 as major components found in the proteomic analysis.

claim: CD9 and CD81 have distinct non-redundant functions in TNT biology.
source: We show that these two tetraspanins have distinct non-redundant functions: CD9 participates in stabilizing TNTs, whereas CD81 expression is required to allow the functional transfer of vesicles in the newly formed TNTs, possibly by regulating docking to or fusion with the opposing cell.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the distinct functions of CD9 and CD81.

claim: CD9 participates in stabilizing TNTs.
source: We show that these two tetraspanins have distinct non-redundant functions: CD9 participates in stabilizing TNTs, whereas CD81 expression is required to allow the functional transfer of vesicles in the newly formed TNTs, possibly by regulating docking to or fusion with the opposing cell.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states CD9's role in TNT stabilization.

claim: CD81 expression is required to allow functional transfer of vesicles in newly formed TNTs.
source: We show that these two tetraspanins have distinct non-redundant functions: CD9 participates in stabilizing TNTs, whereas CD81 expression is required to allow the functional transfer of vesicles in the newly formed TNTs, possibly by regulating docking to or fusion with the opposing cell.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states CD81's role in vesicle transfer.

claim: CD81 possibly regulates docking to or fusion with the opposing cell.
source: We show that these two tetraspanins have distinct non-redundant functions: CD9 participates in stabilizing TNTs, whereas CD81 expression is required to allow the functional transfer of vesicles in the newly formed TNTs, possibly by regulating docking to or fusion with the opposing cell.
evidence: The abstract proposes a mechanism for CD81's function.

claim: TNTs are thin membranous conduits supported by F-actin.
source: Tunneling nanotubes (TNTs) are thin membranous conduits, supported by F-actin that form continuous cytoplasmic bridges between cells over distances ranging from several hundred nm up to 100 µm (Rustom et al., 2004; Sartori-Rupp et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction provides a structural description of TNTs with citations.

claim: TNTs form continuous cytoplasmic bridges between cells over distances ranging from several hundred nm up to 100 µm.
source: Tunneling nanotubes (TNTs) are thin membranous conduits, supported by F-actin that form continuous cytoplasmic bridges between cells over distances ranging from several hundred nm up to 100 µm (Rustom et al., 2004; Sartori-Rupp et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction specifies the distance range of TNTs with supporting citations.

claim: TNTs facilitate transfer of organelles including lysosomes and mitochondria.
source: They allow cell-to-cell communication by facilitating the transfer of different cargoes directly from cytoplasm to cytoplasm of the connected cells, including organelles (e.g. lysosomes, mitochondria) (Abounit et al., 2016; Pinto et al., 2021; Cordero Cervantes and Zurzolo, 2021), micro- or mRNAs, pathogens (Connor et al., 2015; Haimovich et al., 2017) and misfolded/aggregated proteins (e.g. prion proteins, tau, or α-synuclein aggregates Vargas et al., 2019; Dilsizoglu Senol et al., 2021; Chastagner et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction lists organelles as cargo transferred through TNTs with citations.

claim: TNTs facilitate transfer of micro- or mRNAs.
source: They allow cell-to-cell communication by facilitating the transfer of different cargoes directly from cytoplasm to cytoplasm of the connected cells, including organelles (e.g. lysosomes, mitochondria) (Abounit et al., 2016; Pinto et al., 2021; Cordero Cervantes and Zurzolo, 2021), micro- or mRNAs, pathogens (Connor et al., 2015; Haimovich et al., 2017) and misfolded/aggregated proteins (e.g. prion proteins, tau, or α-synuclein aggregates Vargas et al., 2019; Dilsizoglu Senol et al., 2021; Chastagner et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction lists RNAs as cargo transferred through TNTs with citations.

claim: TNTs facilitate transfer of pathogens.
source: They allow cell-to-cell communication by facilitating the transfer of different cargoes directly from cytoplasm to cytoplasm of the connected cells, including organelles (e.g. lysosomes, mitochondria) (Abounit et al., 2016; Pinto et al., 2021; Cordero Cervantes and Zurzolo, 2021), micro- or mRNAs, pathogens (Connor et al., 2015; Haimovich et al., 2017) and misfolded/aggregated proteins (e.g. prion proteins, tau, or α-synuclein aggregates Vargas et al., 2019; Dilsizoglu Senol et al., 2021; Chastagner et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction lists pathogens as cargo transferred through TNTs with citations.

claim: TNTs facilitate transfer of misfolded/aggregated proteins including prion proteins, tau, and α-synuclein aggregates.
source: They allow cell-to-cell communication by facilitating the transfer of different cargoes directly from cytoplasm to cytoplasm of the connected cells, including organelles (e.g. lysosomes, mitochondria) (Abounit et al., 2016; Pinto et al., 2021; Cordero Cervantes and Zurzolo, 2021), micro- or mRNAs, pathogens (Connor et al., 2015; Haimovich et al., 2017) and misfolded/aggregated proteins (e.g. prion proteins, tau, or α-synuclein aggregates Vargas et al., 2019; Dilsizoglu Senol et al., 2021; Chastagner et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction lists misfolded proteins as cargo transferred through TNTs with citations.

claim: TNTs could play major roles in neurodegenerative diseases.
source: TNTs could play major roles in various diseases, including neurodegenerative diseases (Tarasiuk and Scuteri, 2022; Victoria and Zurzolo, 2017; Zurzolo, 2021) or cancers of different types (Pinto et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction states the potential role of TNTs in neurodegenerative diseases with citations.

claim: TNTs could play major roles in cancers of different types.
source: TNTs could play major roles in various diseases, including neurodegenerative diseases (Tarasiuk and Scuteri, 2022; Victoria and Zurzolo, 2017; Zurzolo, 2021) or cancers of different types (Pinto et al., 2020).
evidence: The introduction states the potential role of TNTs in cancers with citations.

claim: TNT-like connections exist in the retina and facilitate cellular material transfer between photoreceptors.
source: In addition to cell cultures and tumor explants (Pinto et al., 2020), TNT-like connections have been shown to exist in the retina and facilitate cellular material transfer between photoreceptors (Kalargyrou et al., 2021; Ortin-Martinez et al., 2021) or pericytes (Alarcon-Martinez et al., 2020), highlighting the importance of understanding the biology of these protrusions in order to unravel their possible role(s) in vivo (Victoria and Zurzolo, 2017).
evidence: The introduction describes TNT-like structures in the retina with citations.

claim: TNT-like connections exist in the retina and facilitate cellular material transfer between pericytes.
source: In addition to cell cultures and tumor explants (Pinto et al., 2020), TNT-like connections have been shown to exist in the retina and facilitate cellular material transfer between photoreceptors (Kalargyrou et al., 2021; Ortin-Martinez et al., 2021) or pericytes (Alarcon-Martinez et al., 2020), highlighting the importance of understanding the biology of these protrusions in order to unravel their possible role(s) in vivo (Victoria and Zurzolo, 2017).
evidence: The introduction describes TNT-like structures in pericytes with citations.

claim: TNT formation is highly dynamic and appears to be regulated by cellular stresses and actin regulators.
source: TNT formation is highly dynamic and appears to be regulated by cellular stresses and actin regulators (Ljubojevic et al., 2021).
evidence: The introduction states the dynamic nature and regulation of TNT formation with citation.

claim: Two models have been proposed for TNT formation: membrane deformation/elongation followed by fusion, or cell dislodgement with fusion preceding elongation.
source: Two models have been proposed for TNT formation. In the first, TNTs would be produced by membrane deformation and elongation of the protrusion supported by actin polymerization followed by adhesion and fusion of this protrusion with the opposing cell. Alternatively, TNTs could be formed by cell dislodgement where adhesion and membrane fusion would be the first steps before cell body separation and elongation of the protrusion by actin polymerization (Ljubojevic et al., 2021; Abounit and Zurzolo, 2012).
evidence: The introduction describes two proposed models for TNT formation with citations.

claim: TNTs are made up of bundles of fine open connections called iTNTs held together by partially identified proteins including N-Cadherin.
source: However, TNTs have been shown to be structurally more complex, being made up of bundles of fine open connections (called iTNTs) held together by partially identified proteins, including N-Cadherin (Sartori-Rupp et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction describes the structural complexity of TNTs with citation.

claim: The mechanism(s) and specific pathways governing iTNT/TNT formation as well as the molecular components of TNTs are still not known.
source: The mechanism(s) and specific pathways governing iTNT/TNT formation as well as the molecular components of TNTs are still not known.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states this knowledge gap.

claim: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are released by all cells and taken up by distant recipient cells.
source: EVs are released by all cells, and up taken by distant recipient cells (Charreau, 2021; van Niel et al., 2022; Wolfers et al., 2001).
evidence: The introduction describes EV biology with citations.

claim: EVs can be formed by direct budding from the plasma membrane or by secretion of intraluminal vesicles of multivesicular compartments (exosomes).
source: They can be formed either by direct budding from the plasma membrane, or by secretion of intraluminal vesicles of multivesicular compartments (in which case they are called exosomes).
evidence: The introduction describes two mechanisms of EV formation.

claim: It has been challenging to distinguish TNTs from EVs in terms of composition due to their common functions, similar diameters, and TNT fragility.
source: Because of their common functions, their similar diameters, and because TNTs are fragile and easily broken and therefore can be released in cell culture supernatants (where EVs are also found), it has been challenging to distinguish TNTs from EVs in terms of composition (Gousset et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction explains the challenge of distinguishing TNTs from EVs with citation.

claim: CD9 and CD81 are well-known and widely used markers for EVs.
source: In this regard, two members of the tetraspanin family, CD9 and CD81, which are well-known and widely used markers for EVs (Théry et al., 2018), have been detected in TNTs in T cells when overexpressed (Lachambre et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction states CD9 and CD81 are EV markers with citation.

claim: CD9 and CD81 have been detected in TNTs in T cells when overexpressed.
source: In this regard, two members of the tetraspanin family, CD9 and CD81, which are well-known and widely used markers for EVs (Théry et al., 2018), have been detected in TNTs in T cells when overexpressed (Lachambre et al., 2014).
evidence: The introduction cites previous detection of CD9 and CD81 in TNTs.

claim: The tetraspanin family has 33 members in mammals.
source: Tetraspanin forms a family (with 33 members in mammals) of small four membrane-spanning domain proteins with two extracellular domains, including a large one harboring a tetraspanin-specific folding and two short cytoplasmic tails.
evidence: The introduction provides information about the tetraspanin family.

claim: Tetraspanins are small four membrane-spanning domain proteins with two extracellular domains and two short cytoplasmic tails.
source: Tetraspanin forms a family (with 33 members in mammals) of small four membrane-spanning domain proteins with two extracellular domains, including a large one harboring a tetraspanin-specific folding and two short cytoplasmic tails.
evidence: The introduction describes the structure of tetraspanins.

claim: Tetraspanins are involved in various cellular processes including migration, adhesion, signaling, pathogen infection, membrane damage reparation, membrane protrusive activity, and cell-cell fusion.
source: Tetraspanins are involved in various cellular processes like migration, adhesion, signaling, pathogen infection, membrane damage reparation, membrane protrusive activity, and cell-cell fusion (Charrin et al., 2009; Charrin et al., 2014; Hemler, 2005; Huang et al., 2018).
evidence: The introduction lists cellular processes involving tetraspanins with citations.

claim: Tetraspanin function is linked to their ability to interact with other transmembrane proteins, forming a dynamic network called the tetraspanin web or Tetraspanin-enriched microdomains (TEM).
source: Their function is linked at least in part to their ability to interact with other transmembrane proteins, forming a dynamic network or molecular interactions referred to as the tetraspanin web or Tetraspanin-enriched microdomains (TEM) (Yáñez-Mó et al., 2009).
evidence: The introduction describes the tetraspanin web with citation.

claim: CD9 and CD81 directly interact with CD9P1 (EWI-F, encoded by PTGFRN gene) and EWI-2 (encoded by IGSF8 gene).
source: Inside this 'web,' the tetraspanins CD9 and CD81 directly interact with the Ig domain proteins CD9P1 (aka EWI-F, encoded by the PTGFRN gene) and EWI-2 (encoded by the IGSF8 gene) (Stipp et al., 2001b; Stipp et al., 2001a; Charrin et al., 2001; Charrin et al., 2003), which have an impact on several fusion processes (Charrin et al., 2013; Cohen et al., 2022; Whitaker et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction describes protein interactions with citations.

claim: CD9P1 and EWI-2 have an impact on several fusion processes.
source: Inside this 'web,' the tetraspanins CD9 and CD81 directly interact with the Ig domain proteins CD9P1 (aka EWI-F, encoded by the PTGFRN gene) and EWI-2 (encoded by the IGSF8 gene) (Stipp et al., 2001b; Stipp et al., 2001a; Charrin et al., 2001; Charrin et al., 2003), which have an impact on several fusion processes (Charrin et al., 2013; Cohen et al., 2022; Whitaker et al., 2019).
evidence: The introduction states the functional impact of CD9P1 and EWI-2 with citations.

claim: Whether CD9 and CD81 are endogenously present in TNTs from non-T lymphoid cells has not been investigated.
source: Whether CD9 and CD81 are also endogenously present in TNTs from non-T lymphoid cells, and whether they play a role in the formation or function of TNTs has not been investigated.
evidence: The introduction identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Whether CD9 and CD81 play a role in the formation or function of TNTs has not been investigated.
source: Whether CD9 and CD81 are also endogenously present in TNTs from non-T lymphoid cells, and whether they play a role in the formation or function of TNTs has not been investigated.
evidence: The introduction identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: A protocol of TNT isolation from U2OS cultured cells was established allowing separation of TNTs from extracellular vesicles and particles (EVPs) and from cell bodies.
source: With the goal of identifying structural components of TNTs, and possibly specific markers and regulators of these structures, we established a protocol of TNT isolation from U2OS cultured cells (Pontén and Saksela, 1967), allowing to separate TNTs from extracellular vesicles and particles (EVPs) and from cell bodies.
evidence: The introduction describes the methodological approach of the study.

claim: The full protein composition of TNTs compared to EVPs was obtained.
source: We obtained the full protein composition of TNTs, compared to EVPs.
evidence: The introduction states a key finding of the study.

claim: CD9 and CD81 have different and complementary functions by possibly regulating two different steps of the formation of TNTs.
source: Our data indicate that CD9 and CD81 have different and complementary functions by possibly regulating two different steps of the formation of TNTs.
evidence: The introduction summarizes the main conclusion of the study.

claim: U2OS cells are robustly adherent cells exhibiting few long protrusions.
source: We used U2OS cells because they are robustly adherent cells exhibiting few long protrusions and are able to grow TNTs in complete and serum-free medium and transfer cellular material through these bridges (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B and Pergu et al., 2019).
evidence: The results section describes characteristics of U2OS cells.

claim: U2OS cells are able to grow TNTs in complete and serum-free medium and transfer cellular material through these bridges.
source: We used U2OS cells because they are robustly adherent cells exhibiting few long protrusions and are able to grow TNTs in complete and serum-free medium and transfer cellular material through these bridges (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B and Pergu et al., 2019).
evidence: The results section describes TNT formation in U2OS cells with citation and figure reference.

claim: TNTs are very sensitive to mechanical stress as they are not attached to the substrate.
source: In order to isolate nanotubes and similar structures (generically referred to hereafter as TNTs), we took advantage of the fact that TNTs are very sensitive to mechanical stress as they are not attached to the substrate (Rustom et al., 2004; Pontes et al., 2008).
evidence: The results section describes a property of TNTs used for isolation with citations.

claim: EVPs appeared mostly circular with a mean diameter of 60 nm.
source: Observation of the obtained particles using transmission electronic microscopy revealed that they were morphologically different (Figure 1B). EVPs appeared mostly circular with a mean diameter of 60 nm (Figure 1C), whereas TNTs (or TNT fragments) were mostly cylindrical, with a mean diameter of 69 nm and length varying from 140 to 900 nm (mean length 372 nm).
evidence: The results section describes TEM observations with figure references.

claim: TNTs (or TNT fragments) were mostly cylindrical, with a mean diameter of 69 nm and length varying from 140 to 900 nm (mean length 372 nm).
source: Observation of the obtained particles using transmission electronic microscopy revealed that they were morphologically different (Figure 1B). EVPs appeared mostly circular with a mean diameter of 60 nm (Figure 1C), whereas TNTs (or TNT fragments) were mostly cylindrical, with a mean diameter of 69 nm and length varying from 140 to 900 nm (mean length 372 nm).
evidence: The results section describes TEM observations with figure references.

claim: Actin chromobody-GFP decorated TNTs after stable expression.
source: As shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, actin chromobody-GFP (an actin-detecting probe that does not affect actin dynamics Melak et al., 2017) decorated TNTs after stable expression.
evidence: The results section describes fluorescent labeling of TNTs with citation and figure reference.

claim: Endogenous CD9 was present on at least a fraction of TNTs formed between U2OS cells.
source: Endogenous CD9 was present on at least a fraction of TNTs formed between U2OS cells (cultured in serum-free or -rich conditions, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and a GFP-CD9 construct also decorated these structures when stably expressed in these cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The results section describes CD9 localization with figure reference.

claim: A GFP-CD9 construct decorated TNTs when stably expressed in U2OS cells.
source: Endogenous CD9 was present on at least a fraction of TNTs formed between U2OS cells (cultured in serum-free or -rich conditions, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), and a GFP-CD9 construct also decorated these structures when stably expressed in these cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The results section describes GFP-CD9 localization with figure reference.

claim: Both EVPs and TNTs contained particles of similar mean diameter (around 60 nm), ranging from 40 to more than 100 nm.
source: As shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C–E, both EVPs and TNTs contained particles of similar mean diameter (around 60 nm, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, D), ranging from 40 to more than 100 nm, in perfect accordance with TEM results.
evidence: The results section describes nanoFCM analysis with figure references.

claim: The sizes and concentrations of EVPs and TNTs were the same in parental and transfected cell lines.
source: The sizes and concentrations of EVPs and TNTs were the same in parental and transfected cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: The results section describes nanoFCM analysis with figure reference.

claim: Both EVP and TNT fractions contained particles bearing GFP-CD9.
source: Both fractions contained particles bearing GFP-CD9 (Figure 1E), confirming the presence of membrane-enclosed particles.
evidence: The results section describes nanoFCM analysis with figure reference.

claim: A major difference between EVP and TNT fractions was the large proportion of particles in the TNT preparation (38%) that bore the actin chromobody-GFP which was barely detected in EVPs (0.2%).
source: A major difference between the two fractions was the large proportion of particles in the TNT preparation (38%) that bore the actin chromobody-GFP which was barely detected in EVPs (0.2%).
evidence: The results section describes a key difference between EVPs and TNTs.

claim: H2B-GFP was present in a very minor part of the particles.
source: Finally, H2B-GFP was present in a very minor part of the particles, and the Golgi marker GM130 was detected neither in EVPs nor in TNTs by western-blot (Figure 1F), showing that contaminations with cell debris or nuclei were limited, thus validating our protocol.
evidence: The results section describes control experiments with figure reference.

claim: The Golgi marker GM130 was detected neither in EVPs nor in TNTs by western-blot.
source: Finally, H2B-GFP was present in a very minor part of the particles, and the Golgi marker GM130 was detected neither in EVPs nor in TNTs by western-blot (Figure 1F), showing that contaminations with cell debris or nuclei were limited, thus validating our protocol.
evidence: The results section describes control experiments with figure reference.

claim: CD9 and CD63 were detected in both TNT and EVP preparations.
source: CD9 and CD63 were detected in both TNT and EVP preparations, whereas tubulin (shown to label a fraction of TNTs in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) was only detected in TNT fraction.
evidence: The results section describes western blot results.

claim: Tubulin was only detected in TNT fraction.
source: CD9 and CD63 were detected in both TNT and EVP preparations, whereas tubulin (shown to label a fraction of TNTs in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) was only detected in TNT fraction.
evidence: The results section describes western blot results with figure reference.

claim: The classical marker of EVPs Alix was mainly detected in the EVP fraction.
source: The classical marker of EVPs Alix was mainly detected in the EVP fraction, and the ER protein calnexin was detected in neither fraction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The results section describes western blot results with figure reference.

claim: The ER protein calnexin was detected in neither EVP nor TNT fraction.
source: The classical marker of EVPs Alix was mainly detected in the EVP fraction, and the ER protein calnexin was detected in neither fraction (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The results section describes western blot results with figure reference.

claim: Shaking the cells did not affect their shape and plate attachment.
source: We checked that shaking the cells did not affect their shape and plate attachment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, 2 left pictures).
evidence: The results section describes control experiments with figure reference.

claim: Shaking decreased the percentage of connections between cells cultured in serum-free medium.
source: In contrast, it decreased the percentage of connections between cells, identified after mild trypsinization and phase image analysis of fixed cells (right pictures and graph of Figure 1—figure supplement 1G) cultured in serum-free medium.
evidence: The results section describes the effect of shaking with figure reference.

claim: Connections were formed in both serum-rich and reduced serum culture conditions.
source: We observed that connections were formed in both culture conditions, and that cell-to-cell transfer was happening in a similar ratio in serum-rich and reduced conditions.
evidence: The results section describes observations in different culture conditions.

claim: Cell-to-cell transfer was happening in a similar ratio in serum-rich and reduced conditions.
source: We observed that connections were formed in both culture conditions, and that cell-to-cell transfer was happening in a similar ratio in serum-rich and reduced conditions.
evidence: The results section describes transfer experiments in different culture conditions.

claim: Serum deprivation did not affect the nature of the TNTs.
source: Together with the expression of several markers in both conditions on these cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), these results confirmed that serum deprivation did not affect the nature of the TNTs.
evidence: The results section concludes about the effect of serum deprivation with figure references.

claim: 1177 proteins were identified in at least nine TNT preparations.
source: 1177 proteins were identified in at least nine preparations (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The results section reports the number of proteins identified in the TNTome.

claim: Proteins previously described in TNTs, like actin, Myosin10, ERp29, or N-cadherin were present in the TNTome.
source: We first observed that proteins previously described in TNTs, like actin, Myosin10 (Gousset et al., 2013), ERp29 (Pergu et al., 2019), or N-cadherin (Sartori-Rupp et al., 2019; Chang et al., 2022) were indeed present in the TNTome.
evidence: The results section validates the TNTome by finding known TNT proteins with citations.

claim: Less than 100 nuclear proteins (less than 8%) were found in the TNTome.
source: Less than 100 nuclear proteins (according to GO Cellular component analysis), i.e., less than 8%, were found, which could result from partial contamination with cellular debris or dead cells.
evidence: The results section reports the proportion of nuclear proteins in the TNTome.

claim: The 1177 proteins have been ranked in four quartiles depending on their relative abundancy (average iBAQ).
source: The 1177 proteins have been ranked in four quartiles depending on their relative abundancy (average iBAQ), highlighting the enrichment of specific factors when considering gene ontology (Supplementary file 1, Figure 2A).
evidence: The results section describes the analysis approach with figure reference.

claim: TNTome is rich in mitochondrial (8% of the total), lysosomal/endosomal or other vesicle proteins.
source: It could be why mitochondrial (8% of the total), lysosomal/endosomal or other vesicle proteins are listed.
evidence: The results section reports the proportion of organellar proteins in the TNTome.

claim: TNTome is rich in RNA-associated proteins (ribosomes, translation factors, ribonucleoproteins).
source: The Proteomap analysis (Figure 2A) also revealed that TNTome is rich in RNA-associated proteins (ribosomes, translation factors, ribonucleoproteins), in accordance with TNTs being able to transfer micro and mRNAs (Haimovich et al., 2021; Kolba et al., 2019).
evidence: The results section describes the composition of the TNTome with figure reference and citations.

claim: A major group of proteins of interest in the TNTome were related to the cytoskeleton (15%, i.e. 172 proteins).
source: A major group of proteins of interest were related to the cytoskeleton (15%, i.e. 172 proteins, see Supplementary file 2, analysis of GO terms, cellular components).
evidence: The results section reports the proportion of cytoskeleton proteins in the TNTome.

claim: Actin-related proteins were majority compared to microtubule-related or intermediate filament-related proteins in the TNTome.
source: As shown by STRING functional network representation, actin-related proteins were majority (Figure 2B, orange nodes) compared to microtubule-related (green nodes) or intermediate filament-related proteins (blue nodes).
evidence: The results section describes the composition of cytoskeleton proteins with figure reference.

claim: Actin was the fourth most abundant protein of TNTome.
source: Actin was the fourth most abundant protein of TNTome, whereas tubulin beta and alpha chains were ranked in positions 6 and 7.
evidence: The results section reports the abundance ranking of cytoskeleton proteins.

claim: Tubulin beta and alpha chains were ranked in positions 6 and 7 in the TNTome.
source: Actin was the fourth most abundant protein of TNTome, whereas tubulin beta and alpha chains were ranked in positions 6 and 7.
evidence: The results section reports the abundance ranking of cytoskeleton proteins.

claim: TNTs, in addition to actin, could contain microtubules as in some cancers.
source: However, recent work has shown that TNTs, in addition to actin, could contain microtubules as in some cancers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Pinto et al., 2020; Lou, 2020), and cytokeratins like in the case of urothelial cells (Resnik et al., 2019; Resnik et al., 2018).
evidence: The results section discusses the presence of microtubules in TNTs with citations and figure reference.

claim: TNTs could contain cytokeratins like in the case of urothelial cells.
source: However, recent work has shown that TNTs, in addition to actin, could contain microtubules as in some cancers (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Pinto et al., 2020; Lou, 2020), and cytokeratins like in the case of urothelial cells (Resnik et al., 2019; Resnik et al., 2018).
evidence: The results section discusses the presence of cytokeratins in TNTs with citations.

claim: Around 500 proteins in the TNTome were classified as membrane-related, 64 of which being strictly integral plasma membranes.
source: When looking at membrane proteins, analysis of the GO terms (cellular components) of the TNTome classified around 500 proteins as membrane-related, 64 of which being strictly integral plasma membranes (see Supplementary file 3 and Figure 2C).
evidence: The results section reports the number of membrane proteins in the TNTome with figure reference.

claim: N-cadherin and other cadherin-related proteins, as well as known N-cadherin interactors like alpha-catenin, were found in the TNTome.
source: Among the latter, N-cadherin and other cadherin-related proteins (green nodes), as well as known N-cadherin interactors like alpha-catenin, were found.
evidence: The results section lists specific membrane proteins found in the TNTome.

claim: Various integrin subunits, including the Integrin β1, were found in the TNTome.
source: We also noticed the presence of various integrin subunits (orange nodes), including the Integrin β1.
evidence: The results section lists specific membrane proteins found in the TNTome.

claim: The TNTome had only a partial overlap with integrin adhesion complexes.
source: However, the TNTome had only a partial overlap with integrin adhesion complexes (Horton et al., 2015, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and tab1 of Supplementary file 4) and with the consensus adhesome (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, tab2 of Supplementary file 4).
evidence: The results section compares the TNTome with known protein complexes with citation and figure reference.

claim: The TNTome had only a partial overlap with the consensus adhesome.
